lines: +An unquoted `font-family` or `font` name stays whole on iOS, Android, and React Native for Web. A name holding a CSS escape reads as a browser reads it, so `A\42 B` names the face `ABB` and `\73 erif` is the generic keyword `serif`. A name starting with a hyphen, such as `-apple-system`, is one name, and a `font` declaration holding one keeps its size and weight. A keyword the library matches, such as `\62 old` in `font`, reads correctly too. A value that reaches React Native as text, such as the color in `color: r\65 d` or `border: 1px solid r\65 d`, keeps the escape as written and isn't read as `red`, and an escape inside a unit (`10\70 x`) isn't read. A vendor-prefixed name in a transition, such as `transition-property: -webkit-transform, opacity`, reads as `transform` at its place in the list. A sign belongs on a number inside math, as in a browser, so `calc(-pi * 1px)` holds the name `-pi` and warns in development, while `calc(-1 * pi * 1px)` resolves.

| `corner-shape: round \| squircle \| square \| superellipse()`                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Three contours are reachable, at very different fidelities. `round` (and `superellipse()` near 1) maps to `borderCurve: circular`, which is React Native's own default, so it is exact everywhere. `square` (and `superellipse(infinity)`) applies a zero radius to the corners it names, which the spec defines as the same shape, so it is also exact everywhere and is the only value Android renders; it may be mixed with one curve (`corner-shape: square round`) because it resolves per corner rather than to the single per-view `borderCurve`. `squircle` (and `superellipse()` near 2) maps to Apple's continuous curve and is a loose approximation: measured on iOS 26, `continuous` moves the outline under 1% of the element's side at any radius, roughly an eighth as far as the exponent-4 superellipse the spec asks for, so expect it to look nearly identical to `round`. Android drops `borderCurve` entirely (it is absent from the Android view config) and warns. Concave and beveled contours (`bevel`, `notch`, `scoop`, out-of-band superellipse values) cannot be drawn at all and drop with a one-time development warning, leaving the initial `round`; two different *curves* on different corners likewise drop, since `borderCurve` is per-view. rn-web passes the value through for browsers that support it (Chrome 139+). Note for React Native 0.85/0.86: `borderCurve` is silently ignored if the `enableCppPropsIteratorSetter` feature flag is turned on, because the C++ props setter has no case for it; the flag defaults off, and the gap is fixed in 0.87. |
